matches.rationale: Ground truth 1 identifies that the abstract overstates TTFT (claiming 4.2× vs actual ~3.5×) and throughput (claiming 3.2–4.5× vs actual ~3.1×) compared to experimental data. Findings 1, 2, and 3 all detect inconsistencies between the abstract's performance claims and Section 4.2's actual results, though they report different specific numbers (6.8× and 5.1–7.2× in findings vs 4.2× and 3.2–4.5× in ground truth). The core issue—abstract inflating performance metrics beyond experimental evidence—is the same.

Ground truth 2 describes a logical inconsistency in Section 3.1 where text contradicts Equation 1's definition of burst tolerance (ratio vs. difference). Finding 8 identifies an issue with Equation 2 in Section 3.2 regarding normalization denominators, which is a different equation and different logical problem. No finding addresses the burst tolerance definition inconsistency.

Ground truth 3 identifies missing experimental protocol details for baseline systems (batch sizes, KV cache settings, etc.) in Section 4.1. None of the findings mention this omission of baseline configuration details. The findings focus on performance claim inconsistencies and methodological issues, not missing experimental setup information.

Ground truth 4 identifies that text accompanying Figure 6 claims throughput gains of 4.5× and 3.2× when the actual data shows ~3.1× and 2.8×. Finding 2 detects that Section 4.2 and Figure 6 report maximum throughput improvements of 'up to 4.5× and 3.2×' which contradicts the abstract's higher claims, capturing the same inflated throughput reporting issue in the ShareGPT-4o results.

Ground truth 5 identifies an unsupported generalization claim in Section 4.2 about 'universal applicability across all MLLM architectures' when only two models were tested. None of the findings mention this overgeneralization about architectural coverage. The findings focus on performance metrics and other claim distortions.

Ground truth 6 describes fabrication of a non-existent reference [61] attributed to 'Zhang et al.' in Section 5 (Related Work). None of the findings mention fabricated references or issues in the Related Work section. The findings focus on performance claims, methodology, and other sections.

Ground truth 7 identifies logical inconsistency between Equations 2 and 3 in Section 3.2, where different penalty factors and cost structures are used without explanation. Finding 8 identifies that Equation 2's gain-cost model uses different denominators (input_len vs output_len) for different request sets, making them incomparable—this is the same underlying issue of inconsistent cost/gain formulation in the optimization framework.

Ground truth 8 identifies omission of ethical considerations regarding dataset collection (user consent, IRB approval, web scraping compliance) in Section 4.1. None of the findings mention ethical issues, data provenance, or consent concerns. The findings focus on technical inconsistencies and performance claims.

Ground truth 9 identifies promotional language in the Introduction claiming ElasticMM 'completely eliminates all inference bottlenecks and solves the multimodal serving problem.' Finding 4 detects the exact same issue in Section 3, identifying the claim as 'a groundbreaking paradigm that completely eliminates all inference bottlenecks and solves the multimodal serving problem' and correctly labels it as an extreme overstatement.

Ground truth 10 identifies that the abstract mischaracterizes 'unified multimodal prefix caching' as part of scheduling (Section 3.2) when it's actually a separate optimization (Section 3.3). None of the findings mention this narrative inconsistency about where prefix caching fits in the system architecture. The findings focus on other types of inconsistencies.

Ground truth 11 identifies that Section 4.3 claims 'both optimizations provide substantial and roughly equal performance gains' when Figure 8 likely shows unequal contributions. Finding 6 mentions Section 4.3 and Figure 7 but focuses on metric inconsistencies (QPM vs RPM), not the relative contribution equality claim. The issues are different.

Ground truth 12 identifies unfair comparison where ElasticMM uses 'optimized CUDA kernels and custom memory allocators not available to baseline systems' in Section 4.1. None of the findings mention implementation advantages or unfair optimization differences between ElasticMM and baselines. The findings focus on other experimental and claim issues.

Ground truth 13 identifies that the Conclusion claims ElasticMM 'guarantees SLO compliance under all workload conditions' when experimental results show conditional compliance only. Finding 5 detects the Conclusion's claim of 'a complete solution to the multimodal serving problem with no significant limitations or risks' and identifies it as an unjustified absolute claim, noting the contradiction with acknowledged limitations—this captures the same distortion of conditional results as absolute guarantees.

Ground truth 14 identifies false attribution in Section 2.1 claiming encoder-decoder MLLM architectures were 'first introduced by Vaswani et al. [10]' when reference [10] is about Transformers for machine translation, not multimodal models. None of the findings mention this misattribution or issues in the Preliminaries section regarding architectural lineage.

Ground truth 15 identifies omission of limitations discussion and societal impact considerations in the Conclusion. While Finding 5 mentions the Conclusion, it focuses on the 'complete solution' claim rather than the absence of limitations/risks discussion. The ground truth is about what's missing (ethical integrity omission), not what's overstated.
